`psa_bool = TRUE` and `n_sim = 1` still produces a PSA output. For replicability, it will always return the same value, as the seed is fixed per simulation to ensure results are consistent. To have a deterministic base case, we would set `psa_bool = FALSE` and `n_sim = 1`. If `psa_bool = FALSE` and `n_sim >1`, then sampling error would be observed (if any). If `psa_bool = TRUE` and `n_sim >1`, then both sampling error and probabilistic variance would be observed.  

$~$

Note that the engine in this version of the package does not incorporate random substreams of numbers to ensure patients would share the same random seed for each specific variable, e.g., imagine we start with a common set-up. If patient in arm A has event 1 in which `time_1 = rexp(1,1)` occurs, and then has event 2 where `time_1 = rexp(1,1.1)` is evaluated, this will give different values for time_1 than a patient in arm B who has event 1 with `time_1 = rexp(1,1)`, event 3 with `time_2 = rexp(1,3)` and then event 2 where `time_1 = rexp(1,1.1)`. This is because the random number changes when we call `time_2`. If the user does not want this to happen, then it's recommended to use substreams (but in this version of the package it's a bit tricky) through `parallel::nextRNGSubStream(.Random.seed)`.  

```{r one}
set.seed(1)
time_1 = rexp(1,1)
print(time_1)
time_1 = rexp(1,1.1)
print(time_1)

print("DIfferent to:")
set.seed(1)
time_1 = rexp(1,1)
print(time_1)

time_2 = rexp(1,3)
time_1 = rexp(1,1.1)
print(time_1)
```
$~$

`modify_item` is not sequential in this current version of the package, so inputs that depend on the previous input will not work as such. The recommended use is therefore slightly different:
```{r two, eval=FALSE}
  #THIS DOES NOT WORK AS INTENDED AS IT EVALUATES AT ONCE
  #modify_item(list(a=1,b=a+1))
  
  a <- 1
  b <- a + 1
  modify_item(list(a=a,b=b))

```

$~$

One should be careful with `round()` as R may round up or down depending on the number being even/odd:
"Note that for rounding off a 5, the IEC 60559 standard (see also ‘IEEE 754’) is expected to be used, ‘go to the even digit’. Therefore round(0.5) is 0 and round(-1.5) is -2."
<https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/base/versions/3.6.2/topics/Round> 

### V2

Just as a note in case of unintended behavior, patient time to events are initialized at the patient-arm level. That means that if we wanted to set the same natural time to death across different interventions, we would need to fix the seed at the patient level in `init_event_list` for `add_tte`, e.g., something like `nat_death = draw_tte(1, dist = "exp", coef1 = 1, seed = i )` with seed set to `i`, which is the patient id and if there are differences by arm, then those can be set by using an approach like `hr = ifelse(arm=="arm_1",1,0.8)`, or by forcing the seeding to be unique for the patient-arm pair (e.g., something like `set.seed(i * which(arm == trt_list))` or similar, it can also be set so that each pair has a unique seed attached to them).

In most cases, setting named vectors does not affect the program. For example, the package automatically unnames utilities/costs as they are processed. The only issue that could occur is with the event times, but since in this code the use is through `draw_tte`, no issues are found. This is just to prevent some extreme use cases, and this warning has been limited in the newest version.

$~$

### V2


Event `"age"` has been defined in the list of `add_reactevt`. However, this event is currently not used, and while it's harmless, it's not really needed. 

$~$

In the reaction to the event `"initialise"` (i.e., in its `add_reactevt`), `"death"` appears within the `modify_item`. However, "death" seems to be an event, not an item, so it should be moved instead to its own category, i.e., in `modify_event`.

$~$

In `"treatment_switch"` event reaction, the note on the non-sequential evaluation nature of `modify_item` applies (`"treatment_line"` is not updated for the `"v_discontinuation_rate"` formula). A proposed solution has been indicated.


## Modular Approach

As R codes: The code `testing/test_descem_rrms_5_1.R` contains two tests performed to evaluate modularization. One using 3 PSA iterations, modular and non-modular, to test results. And one using a single iteration, PSA and non-PSA, to check that results indeed change between both approaches. The testing shows no issues with changing a modular vs non-modular approach.  

$~$

### V2


As functions (inteded use as e.g., `add_item(load_parameter_example())`): the issue of modularization with functions has to do with the environment scoping of the function and the parent environment of the function defined, because the function will be defined in the global environment, so it's parent scope will be the global environment, where `psa_bool` is not defined (as it's defined within `RunSim`). One would need to pass `psa_bool` as an argument for it to work, and even so, it's not really recommended (as it does not look anymore for values in the `input_list` generated, but rather only on the global inputs (except for the parameters passed as arguments), so one would need to pass further arguments for each of the parameters used, which makes it not so advantageous in terms of readability). Alternatively, one could force the environment of the function to be the current environment where it's being evaluated.

```{r four, eval=FALSE}

#JSA: this also works, but every parameter that is used within the function must be passed as an argument,
#or else the function will look for those in the global scope and fail to find them
example_function <- function(psa_bool,u_rrms_edss) {if(psa_bool){u_rrms_edss}else{0}}
common_all_inputs <- common_all_inputs %>% add_item( example_parameter =   example_function(psa_bool,u_rrms_edss))

#JSA:This works because we set the environment of example_function not to be the global environment,
#but rather the environment where the variable is being created
example_function <- function() {if(psa_bool){1}else{0}}
common_all_inputs <- common_all_inputs %>% add_item( example_parameter = {
  environment(example_function) <- environment()
  example_function()
  })

#JSA: In any of the cases we need to set the name of the object to be created first.

```

Finally, it's important to note that in this version of the package the name of the final object must be defined. In the most recent version of the package this has been partially solved by 1) having a specific function defined to select the right values (which even allows to draw from different distributions with different parameter lengths all at once), and 2) by having any user-defined function that returns a named list would work, so something like `return_list = function(psa_bool){list(parameter_1=ifelse(psa_bool,1,0), parameter_2=ifelse(psa_bool,3,4))}; add_item(return_list(psa_bool))` would automatically assign `parameter_1` and `parameter_2` as distinct objects for the inputs without needing to defining them in `add_item`. This means one can vectorize value assignments, making the code run faster.
